title: LangGraph
subtitle: Agents are graphs with state, not chains

slides.title: The thesis
bullets: A chain is a DAG of prompts: fixed at authoring time, no going back
Five things a DAG cannot express: loops, runtime branching, informed retries,
pausing for approval, resuming after a crash
Everyone discovers this the same way: chain -> while loop -> step counter ->
try/except -> a dict of 'stuff so far' -> a bad workflow engine, homemade
slides.notes: This progression is universal. Ask the room if anyone has written that homemade workflow engine -- most hands go up.

slides.title: The bet
slides.quote: Model your agent as a state machine whose transitions are explicit and whose state is persisted after every step.
bullets: Underneath: Pregel -- bulk-synchronous parallel graph execution
Execution proceeds in SUPERSTEPS: all scheduled nodes run, writes merge, repeat
That is why parallel branches join automatically
And why recursion_limit counts supersteps, not node calls
slides.notes: Pregel is Google's graph model. Knowing this explains three otherwise-mysterious LangGraph behaviors at once.

slides.title: State: the part that is actually hard
bullets: Nodes are the easy part -- (state) -> dict. That's it
Reducers decide how a node's write MERGES into existing state
add_messages is the canonical reducer: appends instead of overwriting
State should hold a plan, a budget, a scratchpad, a cursor -- not just messages
If your graph misbehaves, the bug is in your reducers, not your nodes
slides.notes: code/graph_basics.py demonstrates a custom reducer and a max-iteration guard together.

slides.title: Topology: the four ways to route
rows: control flow is fixed; two edges out = parallel
the node itself knows where to go next
fan-out width is only known at runtime
slides.notes: Always pass the path_map to add_conditional_edges -- without it Studio cannot draw your cycle.

slides.title: Cycles: three ways they end, want the first two
bullets: 1. A semantic exit -- no tool calls returned, or judge score >= threshold
2. A budget in state -- if attempts >= MAX: return END. Inspectable, explainable
3. recursion_limit (default 25 supersteps) raises GraphRecursionError
That third one is a CIRCUIT BREAKER, not a design
If it fires in production you already paid for 25 model calls

slides.title: The comparison you actually need
rows: single-turn tools, <5 steps, no approval needed
the ReAct tool-calling loop IS the product
the LLM is one step in a long business workflow
prototypes where the built-in pattern fits exactly
slides.notes: Default path: start with a plain loop. Move to StateGraph the first time someone asks 'can a human check this first' or 'what happened on run 4471'.

slides.title: When NOT to use LangGraph
slides.quote: If your state schema is {input: str, output: str}, you have written a function with extra steps.
bullets: A one-shot classification does not need a graph
A genuinely linear RAG pipeline does not need a graph
Use it when you can actually name what is in the state

slides.title: Persistence, approval, durability
slides.subtitle: The four things that decide whether anyone lets you run this

slides.title: Persistence: one argument, a different system
bullets: compile(checkpointer=saver); invoke(..., thread_id='ticket-4471')
Memory between turns -- the second invoke resumes from stored state
Resume after a crash or deploy -- the thread lives in Postgres, not a process
Interrupts need this -- no checkpointer means nowhere to pause TO
Time travel: get_state_history() replays every superstep
slides.notes: A thread is a lineage; a checkpoint is one immutable snapshot inside it.

slides.title: Human-in-the-loop: what makes agents deployable
bullets: interrupt() stops the graph; invoke() RETURNS -- no blocked worker, no held socket
Resume days later from a different process for zero ongoing cost
Four patterns: approve/reject, edit the action, review a tool call, ask a question
All four are the same primitive: interrupt() plus Command(resume=...)
slides.notes: This is the single feature that turns a demo into something a regulated business can ship.

slides.title: The re-execution trap
slides.quote: Resuming re-runs the node from the top. LangGraph does not freeze a stack frame.
bullets: send_email() before interrupt() fires AGAIN on every resume
Fix: put the side effect in its own node, or make it idempotent
The same rule governs crash recovery -- a node that died is re-run WHOLE
Design every node so running it twice is boring. The most important line here
slides.notes: code/checkpoint_and_interrupt.py section 4 makes the notification fire twice on purpose -- watch it happen.

slides.title: Why governance cares
bullets: An approval gate turns 'the model did something' into
'a named person authorised this at 14:32, and here is the exact state they saw'
That is the difference between a demo and a regulated production system
It is also a defence against prompt-injected tool calls reaching a side effect

slides.title: Multi-agent patterns
slides.notes: The primitives are unremarkable on purpose: subgraphs plus Command(goto=, graph=PARENT).

slides.title: The honest advice
slides.quote: Most multi-agent systems should be one agent with better tools.
bullets: Each extra agent costs a round trip, a serialization boundary, a lossy hand-off
Anthropic's own research system spent ~15x the tokens of a single chat
Worth it there. Absurd for a support bot
Do not split because the org chart has three teams
slides.notes: Use multiple agents only when context genuinely does not fit, subtasks are independent and parallel, or you need per-role permissions/approval.

slides.title: Durable execution and streaming
bullets: Retries at the node level need idempotency keys -- see the re-execution trap
Streaming modes: values, updates, messages, custom -- pick what the UI needs
Stream token-by-token for chat; stream 'updates' for a progress indicator
Observability: LangSmith traces every node, every superstep -- see ../langsmith/

slides.title: Exit check
bullets: Build a StateGraph with a typed reducer and a max-iteration guard
Implement a ReAct agent as an explicit graph with tool-error handling
Add a checkpointer, an interrupt/approval gate, and resume from it
State, out loud, why most multi-agent systems should be one agent
